title: Service contracts matrix for multiregion routing
body:
Purpose:
This note collects a pragmatic, team-aligned matrix of service contracts for the control plane components that participate in routing decisions across regions: the API Gateway (edge), the Orchestrator (control-plane decision engine), and Runtime Adapters (region-specific runtime proxies). The aim is to produce a small set of crisp contracts that teams can implement against so we can reason about ownership, failure modes, and rollout patterns for multi-region customer traffic.

Context and constraints (assumptions):
- We need deterministic behavior when routing by latency, cost, or regulatory constraints (data locality).
- Runtime Adapters may be implemented in different languages/stacks (K8s sidecars, bare-metal proxies, cloud-native endpoints) but must present a consistent API to the Orchestrator.
- API Gateway sits in front of public traffic and implements coarse-grained policy (auth, basic rate limiting, route classification) but delegates finer routing and fallback decisions to the Orchestrator.
- Multi-region has three operational goals: (1) lowest latency when available, (2) graceful degradation to other regions, (3) predictable cost envelopes.

High-level service contract summary (human-readable):
- API Gateway (edge): authenticates, classifies request metadata, attaches route hints (customer, workload, SLO class), and forwards to Orchestrator endpoints. Must implement retry-safe idempotency hints and provide a short-lived route context token for the Orchestrator to resolve.
- Orchestrator (control-plane): consumes route context, evaluates policies (latency/cost/data-residency/tenant overrides), returns an ordered list of candidate runtime endpoints with per-candidate metadata (region, model-variant, expected-latency-bucket, cost-estimate, TTL). Orchestrator must provide a single canonical decision API and a streaming watch API for route updates.
- Runtime Adapters (runtimes): accept forwarded requests from gateways or orchestrator-assigned proxies, report capacity/health and model compatibility, and accept explicit fallback instructions. Runtimes expose a lightweight capability descriptor and a health score API.

Detailed contract fields (to be implemented in OpenAPI + proto):
- requestContext (API Gateway -> Orchestrator): { tenant_id, workload_type, model_family_hint, seq_len_hint, priority_class, trace_id } (note: in implementation this will be compressed into a signed route token).
- decisionResponse (Orchestrator -> Gateway): orderedCandidates: [ { endpoint, region, adapter_id, estimated_p95_ms, token, cost_tier, compatibility_flags } ], fallbackPolicy: { allow_cross_region: bool, failover_order: [] }, decision_ttl_seconds.
- adapterDescriptor (Runtime -> Orchestrator): { adapter_id, region, supported_models_sha, max_concurrent_sessions, kv_cache_supported: bool, quant_profiles: [names], maintenance_window_hint }

Routing precedence rules (operational):
1) Tenant hard constraints (data residency) — highest priority. Orchestrator must enforce and reject candidates that violate hard constraints.
2) SLA tier match — prefer endpoints in same SLA tier.
3) Latency-first mode — prefer candidate with lowest estimated_p95_ms within cost budget.
4) Cost-first mode — prefer lowest cost_tier while keeping expected latency below tenant-defined threshold.
5) Progressive degradation — only cross-region if in-region candidate capacity < 20% and estimated latency increase <= 2x.

Multi-region failure modes and required observable signals:
- Region blackout: runtimes report health=false and adapter heartbeats stop. Orchestrator must mark region unhealthy and propagate failover candidates with decision_ttl=30s until recovery.
- Network partition (edge -> orchestrator): gateway should fall back to last-known-orchestrator-decision for up to 15s and then move to static failover (pre-configured region list).
- Stale capacity information: adapters must provide sequence numbers for descriptors; orchestrator must use only descriptors newer than X (configurable, default 45s).

Operational ownership (who does what):
- API Gateway team (eng-infra/gateway): owns authentication, request classification, generation and signing of route token, public exposure of orchestrator endpoints and failure mode for gateway-initiated fallback. SLA: 99.9% availability for traffic classification and token issuance.
- Orchestrator team (eng-platform-orchestration): owns decision API, policy config store, rollout of new routing logic, and region health aggregation. SLA: 99.95 for decision API in control-plane instances. Responsible for policy change review and migration window coordination.
- Runtime Adapter owners (per-region runtime teams): own adapter implementation, capacity signaling, and model compatibility testing. Responsible for fast health signaling and graceful drain hooks.
- Oncall & escalations: add orchestration-oncall and runtime-region-oncall runbooks. Orchestrator team handles policy/config escalations; runtime owners handle capacity outages.

Deployment and rollout pattern (recommended):
1) Canary policy rollout: Orchestrator supports scoped rollouts by tenant tag and region. Default rollout step: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% over 48h with automatic regression detection on error-rate/latency.
2) Adapter API contract versioning: use semver on capability descriptor. Orchestrator must ignore fields introduced after the contract version if they are not marked required.
3) Blue/green gateway config sync: Gateways should fetch decision API endpoints from service discovery and use signed tokens; avoid in-place parsing changes at edge.

Open decisions (needs triage):
- Should the Orchestrator return a singleBestCandidate by default to simplify gateways, or always return a ranked-list? (tradeoffs: simplicity vs. faster fallback).
- How to represent bursty ephemeral capacity from Dedicated pools vs. Reserved pools in cost-tiering? Need better telemetry definitions.
- What is the canonical format for adapter 'compatibility_flags' to capture quantization variants and sparse kernels?

Short-term action items (next sprint):
- Draft OpenAPI spec for decisionResponse and adapterDescriptor (owner: Priya) — due 2024-10-25.
- Add adapter heartbeat sequence enforcement to orchestrator prototype (owner: Liam) — due 2024-11-08.
- Create canary policy runbook and dashboard (owner: Sofia) — due 2024-11-12.
- Converge on cross-region failover TTL and gateway fallback window in a follow-up design session.

Appendix: quick checklists for implementers
- Gateway implementer checklist: generate route token (signed), attach minimal requestContext, support fallback-to-last-decision for 15s, follow orchestrator-specified retry hints.
- Orchestrator implementer checklist: validate tenant constraints first, return rankedCandidates + TTL, publish decision API healthmetrics (decision_latency_p95, decision_error_rate), offer watch/stream endpoint.
- Runtime adapter checklist: publish adapterDescriptor on startup, maintain heartbeat every 10s, provide current load and p95 latency estimate, support graceful drain via maintenance_window_hint.

Notes and references:
- This is intentionally practical and scoped — the goal is to reduce ambiguity between teams and unblock implementation. Longer-term we’ll extract a formal spec and wire up compatibility tests in CI.
- See linked artifacts for prior context and the policy store proposal.

Unresolved and low-priority ideas (parking lot):
- Evaluate using weighted randomized decision for traffic-splitting experiments vs deterministic hash-based selection.
- Consider an 'adapter capability registry' service to avoid repeated descriptor polling.

If you are reviewing: please comment on the precedence rules and the suggested failover windows. If you want to own one of the short-term actions, add your name in the collaborators list and ping on #platform-routing.
